Short-Term Air Passenger Demand Forecasting via Adaptive Holt's Linear Trend Method¶

AeroCast — project report and analysis¶

Course: Applied Time Series Analysis (ATSA)

Team: Riti Shah · Pradhi Kanani · Shreeya

Date: 21 October 2026

In one sentence. We forecast daily passenger demand at seven major U.S. airports with AR-Holt, a damped Holt's linear trend method whose smoothing parameter adapts to shocks and whose updates are protected from one-off outliers, and we test it honestly against seven benchmarks — in normal times, during the COVID-19 collapse, and on two classic textbook series.

Contents. 2 Problem · 3 Data · 4 EDA · 5 Decomposition · 6 Stationarity · 7 Theory · 8 Implementation check · 9 Fitted parameters · 10 How the model adapts · 11 Residual diagnostics · 12 Results · 13 Application · 14 Conclusions · 15 References

2. Problem statement and motivation¶

Why short-term demand matters. Airports and airlines plan on a days-to-weeks horizon: how many security lanes to open tomorrow morning, how many officers to roster next week, whether to up-gauge an aircraft or add a frequency. Under-forecasting creates queues and missed connections; over-forecasting wastes staff hours and seats. A forecast with an honest range (prediction interval) lets planners choose a safety margin — e.g. staff to the 80th percentile of demand.

Why fixed smoothing fails under shocks. Exponential smoothing methods (SES, Holt, Holt–Winters) update their level with a fixed weight $\alpha$ on the newest error:

  • a small $\alpha$ gives smooth, stable forecasts in normal times, but reacts very slowly when demand collapses (COVID-19: −95% within weeks) — the model keeps forecasting pre-crisis traffic for weeks;
  • a large $\alpha$ reacts fast, but then chases every one-off spike or dip (Thanksgiving, a snowstorm) and becomes noisy.

No single $\alpha$ is right for both. Our idea (AR-Holt): let $\alpha$ move — small in calm periods, large during persistent shifts — using the tracking signal to tell the two apart, and clip isolated outliers so that a single holiday cannot drag the level, unless the shift turns out to be persistent.

Research questions.

  1. Does AR-Holt forecast better than fixed-parameter Holt variants during a structural shock (COVID-19)?
  2. Does it lose accuracy in normal operations, where adaptivity is not needed?
  3. Which ingredient (adaptive $\alpha$, robust clipping) contributes where?
  4. Are its prediction intervals well calibrated?

3. Data description¶

Dataset Frequency Source
TSA checkpoint throughput, 7 hub airports (ATL, DFW, DEN, ORD, LAX, JFK, SEA) hourly → daily U.S. Transportation Security Administration FOIA reading room (public domain), parsed to CSV by the open-source repository mikelor/TsaThroughput
AirPassengers (Box & Jenkins) monthly R datasets, via vincentarelbundock/Rdatasets
Australian air passengers (Hyndman & Athanasopoulos, FPP3) annual R fpp3, via vincentarelbundock/Rdatasets

Processing (scripts/prepare_data.py): the daily total of an airport is the sum over all of its checkpoints and hours. The same few days are missing for every airport; each missing day is filled with the average of the same weekday one week before and one week after, and flagged imputed = 1. ALL7 is the sum of the seven airports. Genuine shocks (COVID, holidays, storms) are not removed — they are exactly what an adaptive model must handle.

4.3 The COVID collapse and recovery¶

Traffic as a percentage of the same weekday 52 weeks earlier would be distorted after 2020, so we compare every day with the same weekday of 2019 (364 days × k earlier).

In [6]:
s, _ = load_series("ALL7")
base = s["2019-01-01":"2019-12-31"]
ratio = {}
for k, yr in [(1, "2020"), (2, "2021"), (3, "2022"), (4, "2023")]:
    cur = s[yr]
    ref = s.shift(364 * k)[yr]
    ratio[yr] = 100 * cur / ref

5. Decomposition¶

STL (Seasonal-Trend decomposition using LOESS) on the daily ALL7 series with period 7 and robust weights, so holiday spikes end up in the remainder instead of distorting the trend. We show the last two years for readability. Classical multiplicative decomposition on AirPassengers shows a seasonal amplitude that grows with the level — the reason we use multiplicative seasonal indices.

In [8]:
from statsmodels.tsa.seasonal import STL, seasonal_decompose
s, _ = load_series("ALL7")
stl = STL(s, period=7, robust=True).fit()
part = slice("2023-06-01", "2025-05-31")
fig, axes = plt.subplots(4, 1, figsize=(11, 8), sharex=True)
for ax, (name, comp) in zip(axes, [("observed", s), ("trend", stl.trend), ("seasonal (weekly)", stl.seasonal), ("remainder", stl.resid)]):
    ax.plot(comp[part].index, comp[part], color=COL["Holt"] if name != "remainder" else MUTED, lw=1)
    ax.set_title(name, loc="left", fontsize=10)
    thousands(ax)
fig.suptitle("STL decomposition, All 7 hubs (period 7, robust)", x=0.01, ha="left", fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout()
save(fig, "05_stl_all7")
var_r = stl.resid.var()
print(f"Strength of weekly seasonality  F_S = {max(0, 1 - var_r / (stl.seasonal + stl.resid).var()):.3f}")
print(f"Strength of trend               F_T = {max(0, 1 - var_r / (stl.trend + stl.resid).var()):.3f}")

6. Stationarity¶

We run two complementary tests:

  • ADF (Augmented Dickey–Fuller): $H_0$ = unit root (non-stationary). Small p ⇒ stationary.
  • KPSS: $H_0$ = (level-)stationary. Small p ⇒ non-stationary.

They agree when ADF rejects and KPSS does not (stationary), or vice versa. (KPSS p-values are reported by statsmodels only inside [0.01, 0.10]; values at the edge mean "at most" / "at least".)

In [10]:
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import adfuller, kpss

def tests(x, name):
    x = pd.Series(x).dropna()
    adf_stat, adf_p = adfuller(x, autolag="AIC")[:2]
    with warnings.catch_warnings():  # KPSS warns when p is outside its table
        warnings.simplefilter("ignore")
        kpss_stat, kpss_p = kpss(x, regression="c", nlags="auto")[:2]
    adf_says = "stationary" if adf_p < 0.05 else "unit root"
    kpss_says = "non-stationary" if kpss_p < 0.05 else "stationary"
    if adf_says == "stationary" and kpss_says == "stationary":
        verdict = "stationary (both agree)"
    elif adf_says == "unit root" and kpss_says == "non-stationary":
        verdict = "non-stationary (both agree)"
    else:
        verdict = "inconclusive / trend- or difference-stationary"
    return {"series": name, "ADF stat": adf_stat, "ADF p": adf_p, "KPSS stat": kpss_stat,
            "KPSS p": kpss_p, "verdict": verdict}

s, _ = load_series("ALL7")
rows = [tests(s, "ALL7 raw"), tests(np.log(s), "ALL7 log"), tests(np.log(s).diff(), "ALL7 Δ log"),
        tests(np.log(s).diff(7), "ALL7 Δ7 log (weekly diff)"),
        tests(ap, "AirPassengers raw"), tests(np.log(ap), "AirPassengers log"),
        tests(np.log(ap).diff(), "AirPassengers Δ log"), tests(np.log(ap).diff().diff(12), "AirPassengers Δ Δ12 log")]
stat_tab = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("series")
display(stat_tab.style.format({"ADF stat": "{:.2f}", "ADF p": "{:.4f}", "KPSS stat": "{:.3f}", "KPSS p": "{:.3f}"}))

Interpretation. The levels (raw and log) of both series are not stationary — the trend and the COVID break move the mean. For the daily series one difference is enough; for monthly AirPassengers the first difference is still inconclusive because of the strong yearly pattern, and a further seasonal difference is needed. This is why a trend model (Holt) — which forecasts the change via $b_t$ — is natural here, rather than a model that assumes a constant mean. The ACF/PACF of the differenced log series below show strong spikes at lags 7, 14, 21, … — the weekly seasonality we remove with seasonal indices before applying Holt.

7. Theory: from SES to AR-Holt¶

Seasonal adjustment first. Holt's method has no seasonal term, so we model the seasonally adjusted series $x_t = y_t / s_{j(t)}$, where $s_j$ is the multiplicative index of season position $j$ (weekday or month): the median of $y_t / \text{CMA}_t$ over the trailing window, normalised to mean 1. Forecasts are multiplied back: $\hat y_{t+h} = \hat x_{t+h}\, s_{j(t+h)}$.

7.1 Simple exponential smoothing (SES)¶

$$\ell_t = \alpha x_t + (1-\alpha)\,\ell_{t-1}, \qquad \hat x_{t+h|t} = \ell_t$$ A weighted average with geometrically decaying weights. Flat forecasts — no trend.

7.2 Holt's linear trend method (Holt 1957)¶

$$\ell_t = \alpha x_t + (1-\alpha)(\ell_{t-1}+b_{t-1})$$ $$b_t = \beta(\ell_t-\ell_{t-1}) + (1-\beta)\,b_{t-1}$$ $$\hat x_{t+h|t} = \ell_t + h\,b_t$$ Added: a trend $b_t$. Problem: the trend is extrapolated forever — after a collapse, Holt projects the collapse further (forecasts can even go negative).

7.3 Damped trend (Gardner & McKenzie 1985)¶

$$\ell_t = \alpha x_t + (1-\alpha)(\ell_{t-1}+\phi b_{t-1}), \quad b_t = \beta(\ell_t-\ell_{t-1}) + (1-\beta)\phi\, b_{t-1}$$ $$\hat x_{t+h|t} = \ell_t + (\phi+\phi^2+\dots+\phi^h)\, b_t, \qquad \phi\in[0.80, 1]$$ Added: $\phi<1$ makes the trend fade, so long-horizon forecasts flatten. Empirically one of the most robust exponential-smoothing variants.

Error-correction form. With the one-step forecast $\hat x_t = \ell_{t-1}+\phi b_{t-1}$ and error $e_t = x_t - \hat x_t$, damped Holt is equivalently $$\ell_t = \hat x_t + \alpha e_t, \qquad b_t = \phi b_{t-1} + \alpha\beta\, e_t .$$ This form makes it obvious where to intervene: the step size $\alpha$ and the error $e_t$.

7.4 Adaptive response rate (Trigg & Leach 1967)¶

Smoothed error and smoothed absolute error give a tracking signal: $$E_t = \gamma e_t + (1-\gamma)E_{t-1}, \quad M_t = \gamma|e_t| + (1-\gamma)M_{t-1}, \quad TS_t = E_t/M_t \in[-1,1]$$ $|TS_t|\approx 0$ when errors alternate in sign (noise); $|TS_t|\to 1$ when errors are persistently one-signed (the model is biased — a shift). ARR sets $\alpha_t = |TS_{t-1}|$ (clipped to [0.05, 0.95]). Problem: $\alpha_t$ jumps around and is very noisy; one big holiday error both moves the level and inflates $TS$.

7.5 AR-Holt — the proposed Adaptive Robust Holt¶

AR-Holt combines four published ideas: the tracking signal (Trigg & Leach 1967), a smooth transition between parameter regimes (Taylor 2004), Huber-type robust cleaning of errors (Gelper, Fried & Croux 2010) and the damped trend (Gardner & McKenzie 1985). For $t=1,\dots,n$:

$$\hat x_t = \ell_{t-1} + \phi b_{t-1}, \qquad e_t = x_t - \hat x_t$$

$$\text{regime}_t = \begin{cases}\text{shock} & |TS_{t-1}| \ge \tau\\ \text{calm} & \text{otherwise}\end{cases} \qquad \tilde e_t = \begin{cases} e_t & \text{shock}\\ \sigma_{t-1}\,\psi_k\!\left(e_t/\sigma_{t-1}\right) & \text{calm}\end{cases},\quad \psi_k(z)=\max(-k,\min(k,z))$$

$$\alpha_t = \operatorname{expit}\!\big(a + b\,|TS_{t-1}|\big) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-(a+b|TS_{t-1}|)}}$$

$$\ell_t = \hat x_t + \alpha_t\tilde e_t, \qquad b_t = \phi b_{t-1} + \alpha_t\beta\,\tilde e_t$$

$$\sigma_t = \lambda|\tilde e_t| + (1-\lambda)\sigma_{t-1}$$

$$E_t = \gamma\tilde e_t+(1-\gamma)E_{t-1},\quad M_t = \gamma|\tilde e_t|+(1-\gamma)M_{t-1},\quad TS_t = E_t/M_t$$

Forecast: $\hat x_{n+h} = \ell_n + (\phi+\dots+\phi^h)\,b_n$.

What each piece does.

  • Smooth transition — calm $\alpha = \operatorname{expit}(a)$; as $|TS|\to1$, $\alpha\to\operatorname{expit}(a+b)$. $b\ge0$ guarantees $\alpha$ can only rise under bias. Unlike ARR, $\alpha_t$ is a smooth function with two fitted parameters, so it is stable in calm periods.
  • Robust clipping (calm only) — an isolated error larger than $k\sigma$ (e.g. Thanksgiving) moves the level by at most $\alpha k\sigma$; such points are flagged as outliers.
  • Regime switch — if errors stay one-signed, $|TS|$ crosses $\tau$ after a few steps, clipping is switched off and the full error is used: a persistent shift is not an outlier. The clipped errors also feed $TS$, so a single outlier cannot trigger the shock regime by itself.
  • Running scale $\sigma_t$ — sets the clipping threshold and makes the prediction intervals widen automatically after shocks (Section 12).

Parameters. Fitted by minimising the one-step-ahead SSE after a burn-in of $2m$ points (Nelder–Mead, 3 starting points, parameters mapped through logit/softplus so the constraints always hold): $a\in\mathbb R$, $b\ge0$ (softplus), $\beta\in(0,1)$ (logit), $\phi\in[0.80,1]$. Fixed a-priori (not tuned on the test data): $\gamma=0.15,\ k=2.5,\ \lambda=0.1,\ \tau=0.5$.

Interpretation note: the build specification lists "$a, b \ge 0$". We constrain only $b$: forcing $a\ge0$ would force calm $\alpha \ge 0.5$, i.e. a nervous model in normal times, which contradicts the purpose of the calm regime. $a$ is therefore unconstrained.

Initialisation (all smoothing models): $\ell_0 = \bar x_{1..m}$, $b_0 = (\bar x_{m+1..2m}-\bar x_{1..m})/m$, $\sigma_0 = 1.4826\cdot\text{MAD}(\Delta x_{1..2m})$, $E_0=0$, $M_0=\sigma_0$, $TS_0=0$; $m=7$ (daily), 12 (monthly), 3 (annual).

Nesting. With $b=0$ and $k=\infty$, $\alpha_t\equiv\operatorname{expit}(a)$ and no error is ever clipped, so AR-Holt is exactly damped Holt (verified to machine precision in tests/test_models.py::test_ar_holt_nests_damped_holt). AR-Holt can therefore never be structurally worse than damped Holt in-sample; it only adds flexibility.

Prediction intervals — locally-adaptive split conformal. For the last $N$ training origins ($N=365$ daily, 36 monthly, all for annual) compute standardised $h$-step errors $z_{t,h} = (x_{t+h}-\hat x_{t+h|t})/\sigma_t$, take their empirical quantiles $q_h$ (10%/90% for 80%, 2.5%/97.5% for 95%), and set the interval $\big(\hat x_{n+h} + q_h\sigma_n\big)\, s_{j(n+h)}$. No normality assumption; width scales with the current $\sigma_n$. Other models use an EWMA ($\lambda=0.1$) of their own absolute one-step errors as $\sigma_t$.

8. Implementation check: from-scratch Holt vs statsmodels¶

Our Holt is written from scratch in numpy. We check it against statsmodels' Holt on the FPP3 textbook example (Australian air passengers), with the same initial states:

  1. Same parameters — both run with our fitted $\alpha, \beta$: the fitted values and forecasts must be identical (pure recursion check).
  2. Each optimises its own parameters — ours minimises SSE after a burn-in, statsmodels over all points, so small differences are expected.
In [12]:

    smoothing_level=ours.params_["alpha"], smoothing_trend=ours.params_["beta"], optimized=False)
sm_opt = SMHolt(x, initialization_method="known", initial_level=ours.l0_, initial_trend=ours.b0_).fit()
_, run = holt_filter(x, ours.params_["alpha"], ours.params_["beta"], 1.0, ours.l0_, ours.b0_)

Reading the parameters.

  • Calm α vs shock α. Calm α is moderate — the model trusts a new observation only partially in normal times. As the tracking signal approaches 1 the step size rises towards the shock value, so the level catches up with a persistent shift much faster.
  • φ. The damping parameter sits well below 1 for the airports: trends fade within days, which matches the mean-reverting behaviour of daily traffic around a slowly changing level.
  • β. The trend smoothing is tiny: the daily trend changes slowly; most adaptation happens through the level.
  • b ≈ 0 on some series. When the training data contain no persistent shocks (Experiment B trains on 14 calm months), the SSE gives no reason to raise α, and the optimiser sets b to about 0. Adaptivity is learnt from past shocks; when there were none, AR-Holt falls back to a robust damped Holt. This matters for the results in Section 12.
  • Annual data. For the Australian series the optimum is α at its upper limit (each new year fully replaces the level) — the same answer as the textbook Holt fit — so AR-Holt has nothing to adapt.

10. How the model adapts: α_t and the tracking signal, 2019–2025 (key plot)¶

10.2 Are the known events detected?¶

We check the events listed in the data description against the event tables of the series where they happened (each airport fitted on its own full history).

In [17]:
checks = [("COVID collapse", "ALL7", "2020-03-15"), ("COVID collapse", "ATL", "2020-03-20"),
          ("Winter storm (Texas)", "DFW", "2021-02-17"), ("Blizzard", "DEN", "2021-03-14"),
          ("Nor'easter", "JFK", "2021-02-01"), ("Blizzard", "JFK", "2022-01-29")]
for yr, day in [(2021, "11-25"), (2022, "11-24"), (2023, "11-23"), (2024, "11-28")]:
    checks.append((f"Thanksgiving {yr}", "ALL7", f"{yr}-{day}"))
fits = {}
rows = []
for what, series, day in checks:
    if series not in fits:
        y_, _ = load_series(series)
        m_ = AdaptiveRobustHolt().fit(y_, freq="D")
        fits[series] = (m_.components_, event_table(m_.components_))
    comp, evs = fits[series]
    d = pd.Timestamp(day)
    starts, ends = pd.to_datetime(evs.start), pd.to_datetime(evs.end)
    near = evs[(starts <= d + pd.Timedelta(days=2)) & (ends >= d - pd.Timedelta(days=2))]
    rows.append({"event": what, "series": series, "date": day,
                 "detected as": ", ".join(sorted(set(near.type))) or "—",
                 "regime on the day": comp.loc[d, "regime"], "α on the day": comp.loc[d, "alpha"],
                 "one-step error %": 100 * comp.loc[d, "error"] / (comp.loc[d, "adjusted"] - comp.loc[d, "error"])})

1 COVID collapse ATL 2020-03-20 Regime shift shock 0.330 -36.9
2 Winter storm (Texas) DFW 2021-02-17 Outlier calm 0.246 -50.1

9 Thanksgiving 2024 ALL7 2024-11-28 Outlier shock 0.356 -43.5

Discussion. The COVID collapse appears as a long regime shift — exactly what the design intends: clipping switched off and α raised for weeks. The storm days appear as one-day outliers in the calm regime: their errors were clipped, so the level was protected from them.

Thanksgiving is more subtle. It is a multi-day pattern: busy Tuesday/Wednesday, a deep dip on Thursday, a busy Sunday after. The run-up days produce several same-signed errors, which push the tracking signal over τ, so on Thanksgiving Day itself the model is already in the shock regime and the dip is not clipped (the neighbouring days are flagged as outliers). In other words, holiday weeks are partly mistaken for short shifts — a concrete argument for explicit holiday effects (future work). The event tables also show the model's honest weakness: in the noisier post-COVID years many short (3–5 day) shock runs appear. Their average error is small — they are the tracking signal reacting to ordinary week-to-week drift, when |TS| briefly exceeds τ = 0.5. They are harmless for accuracy (α rises only modestly) but they mean that "regime shift" in this table should be read as "the model sped up", not necessarily as a real-world event.

10.3 Robustness of the fixed hyperparameters (validation window only)¶

γ, k, λ, τ were fixed a priori and not tuned. To show that the results do not hinge on them, we vary τ and k on a validation window inside the Experiment A training data: fit on data up to 2023-12-02, evaluate one-step and 7-step forecasts over the last 26 weeks of training (2023-12-03 → 2024-05-31). The test year is never touched.

10.4 Sudden versus gradual shocks (synthetic experiment)¶

A controlled experiment shows when adaptivity pays off. We simulate 500 days with a few earlier level steps and holiday-like outliers, fit both models on the first 400 days, then roll through an unseen −60% shock with parameters fixed. The shock is either instantaneous or spread over 7 or 14 days (COVID-like). We count in how many of 10 random seeds AR-Holt has the lower mean absolute one-step error over the 30 days after the shock starts.

In [19]:
def synthetic(seed, ramp):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    n = 500
    lvl = np.full(n, 10_000.0); lvl[100:] *= 1.25; lvl[220:] *= 0.70; lvl[330:] *= 1.20
    drop = np.ones(n); drop[400:] = 0.4
    if ramp > 1:
        drop[400:400 + ramp] = np.linspace(1, 0.4, ramp + 1)[1:]
    y = lvl * drop * (1 + rng.normal(0, 0.02, n))
    spikes = rng.choice(np.r_[10:395, 440:500], 15, replace=False)
    y[spikes] *= rng.choice([0.6, 1.35], 15)
    return pd.Series(y, index=pd.date_range("2022-01-01", periods=n, freq="D"))

def mae_window(model, y, a, b):
    p_ = model.paths(y, 1)
    return np.abs(p_["x"][a + 1:b + 1] - p_["adj"][a:b, 0]).mean()

rows = []
for label, ramp, (a, b) in [("instant drop, days 1–30", 1, (400, 430)), ("instant drop, days 4–30", 1, (403, 430)),
                            ("7-day decline, days 1–30", 7, (400, 430)), ("14-day decline, days 1–30", 14, (400, 430))]:
    wins, ratio = 0, []
    for seed in range(10):
        y_ = synthetic(seed, ramp)
        h_ = Holt().fit(y_.iloc[:400], freq="D"); r_ = AdaptiveRobustHolt().fit(y_.iloc[:400], freq="D")
        e_h, e_r = mae_window(h_, y_, a, b), mae_window(r_, y_, a, b)
        wins += e_r < e_h; ratio.append(e_r / e_h)
    rows.append({"scenario": label, "AR-Holt wins (of 10)": wins, "median MAE ratio AR/Holt": np.median(ratio)})
display(pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("scenario").style.format({"median MAE ratio AR/Holt": "{:.2f}"}))
  AR-Holt wins (of 10) median MAE ratio AR/Holt
scenario    
instant drop, days 1–30 4 1.10
instant drop, days 4–30 8 0.57
7-day decline, days 1–30 10 0.51
14-day decline, days 1–30 10 0.42

Interpretation — an honest trade-off. On the first day of an instantaneous drop AR-Holt cannot know whether it is facing an outlier or a shift, so it clips the error and waits until the tracking signal confirms the shift (about 2–3 steps). Holt moves immediately. Over the very first days AR-Holt therefore loses; once the shift is confirmed, it re-levels much faster. For gradual collapses — which is how COVID actually unfolded at airports — AR-Holt wins clearly.

11. Residual diagnostics¶

One-step residuals of AR-Holt fitted on the Experiment A training data, expressed as % of the forecast, for the post-COVID part of the training span (2022-06-01 → 2024-05-31) so the collapse does not dominate. A well-specified model should leave white-noise residuals.

In [20]:
from statsmodels.stats.diagnostic import acorr_ljungbox
from scipy import stats as sst
s, _ = load_series("ALL7")
ar_a = AdaptiveRobustHolt().fit(s[:"2024-05-31"], freq="D")
ca = ar_a.components_["2022-06-01":"2024-05-31"]
resid_pct = 100 * ca["error"] / (ca["adjusted"] - ca["error"])
lb = acorr_ljungbox(resid_pct, lags=[7, 14, 28], return_df=True)
display(lb.rename(columns={"lb_stat": "Ljung–Box Q", "lb_pvalue": "p-value"}).style.format({"Ljung–Box Q": "{:.1f}", "p-value": "{:.2g}"}))
print(f"residual mean {resid_pct.mean():+.2f}%, sd {resid_pct.std():.2f}%, skewness {sst.skew(resid_pct):.2f}, "
      f"excess kurtosis {sst.kurtosis(resid_pct):.2f}")
jb = sst.jarque_bera(resid_pct)
print(f"Jarque–Bera normality test: statistic {jb.statistic:.0f}, p = {jb.pvalue:.2g}")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 3.6))
axes[0].hist(resid_pct, bins=60, color=COL["Holt"], edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.5)
axes[0].set_title("histogram of residuals (%)", loc="left"); axes[0].set_xlabel("% error")
(osm, osr), (slope, icpt, _) = sst.probplot(resid_pct, dist="norm")
axes[1].scatter(osm, osr, s=6, color=COL["Holt"]); axes[1].plot(osm, slope * osm + icpt, color=COL["AR-Holt"])
axes[1].set_title("normal Q–Q plot", loc="left"); axes[1].set_xlabel("theoretical quantile")
plot_acf(resid_pct, lags=28, ax=axes[2], color=COL["Holt"], vlines_kwargs={"colors": COL["Holt"]})
axes[2].set_title("ACF of residuals", loc="left"); axes[2].set_xlabel("lag (days)")
fig.tight_layout()
save(fig, "10_residual_diagnostics")
  Ljung–Box Q p-value
7 175.4 1.8e-34
14 200.4 4.5e-35
28 238.8 2.5e-35 
residual mean +0.15%, sd 6.59%, skewness -0.81, excess kurtosis 8.35
Jarque–Bera normality test: statistic 2201, p = 0

Interpretation. The residuals are centred near zero but are not white noise: Ljung–Box rejects at weekly lags and the tails are much heavier than normal (holidays). This is expected for a model with no holiday regressors and a fixed weekday pattern that drifts over the year. Two consequences: (1) there is room for improvement via holiday effects (future work); (2) Gaussian prediction intervals would be wrong — which is exactly why we use conformal intervals calibrated on the model's own empirical errors.

12. Results (from results/, produced by scripts/run_backtests.py)¶

Protocol: parameters and seasonal indices fitted once on the training span; states rolled forward through the test period with parameters fixed; forecasts from every daily origin for h = 1..H; metrics averaged over horizons. MASE is scaled by the in-sample seasonal-naive MAE. Lower is better for every metric except coverage (target: 0.80 and 0.95).

12.4 Accuracy by horizon (All 7 hubs)¶

In [24]:
def dodge(values, gap):
    # Shift label y-positions apart so direct labels never overlap.
    order_ = np.argsort(values); out = np.array(values, float)
    for i in range(1, len(order_)):
        prev, cur = order_[i - 1], order_[i]
        out[cur] = max(out[cur], out[prev] + gap)
    return out

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4.6))
for ax, exp, title in [(axes[0], "A", "Exp A: normal operations"), (axes[1], "B", "Exp B: COVID stress test")]:

    labels = []
    for m in order:
        q = d[d.model == m]
        main = m in ("AR-Holt", "Holt", "DampedHolt", "HoltWinters")
        ax.plot(q.h, q.MAPE, color=COL[m], ls=STYLE.get(m, "-"), lw=2.2 if m == "AR-Holt" else (1.6 if main else 1.1),
                marker="o" if m == "AR-Holt" else None, ms=4, label=m, zorder=3 if m == "AR-Holt" else 2)
        if main:
            labels.append((m, q.h.iloc[-1], q.MAPE.iloc[-1]))
    if exp == "A":  # the Naive model is far above the rest; keep the scale readable
        top = d[d.model != "Naive"].MAPE.max() * 1.08

        ax.text(1, top * 0.985, "Naive is off the top of the scale", fontsize=8.5, color=MUTED, va="top")
    lo, hi = ax.get_ylim()

    for (m, xh, _), yl in zip(labels, ys):
        ax.annotate(m, (xh, yl), xytext=(6, 0), textcoords="offset points", fontsize=8.5, color=INK, va="center")
    ax.set_title(title, loc="left"); ax.set_xlabel("horizon h (days)"); ax.set_ylabel("MAPE (%)")

12.5 Diebold–Mariano tests¶

$H_0$: AR-Holt and the competitor have equal expected loss. HLN small-sample correction, Newey–West variance with lag h−1, t distribution with n−1 df. A negative statistic means AR-Holt has the lower loss. First the All-7 series; then a count over all 8 daily series.

12.7 Ablation study (All 7 hubs)¶

  • COVID stress test (Exp B), ALL7: AR-Holt MAPE 15.41% vs Holt 25.21%, DampedHolt 19.78%, Holt–Winters 18.94%; best model: AR-Holt (15.41%). AR-Holt is best at 4 of 7 airports. AR-Holt vs classic Holt on ALL7: +38.9% relative MAPE reduction.
  • normal operations (Exp A), ALL7: AR-Holt MAPE 6.79% vs Holt 7.03%, DampedHolt 6.76%, Holt–Winters 6.44%; best model: HoltWinters (6.44%). AR-Holt is best at 2 of 7 airports. AR-Holt vs classic Holt on ALL7: +3.3% relative MAPE reduction.
  • Ablation, Exp B: DampedHolt 19.78% → robust only 18.69% → adaptive only 19.78% → full 15.41%.
  • Ablation, Exp A: DampedHolt 6.76% → robust only 6.78% → adaptive only 6.71% → full 6.79%.
  • C1: AR-Holt 5.50%, Holt 5.41%, best HoltWinters 5.34%.
  • C2: AR-Holt 9.49%, Holt 8.71%, best HoltWinters 7.05%.
  • Interval coverage (AR-Holt, ALL7): 80% intervals cover 78.9% (A) / 73.2% (B); 95% intervals cover 94.3% (A) / 92.7% (B).

Discussion.

  • Under a structural shock (Exp B) AR-Holt gives the lowest error on the combined series and at most airports, and classic Holt is clearly the worst smoothing model: its undamped trend extrapolates the collapse. Most of AR-Holt's one-step advantage is statistically significant (DM test); at h = 7 the differences are mostly not significant — over a week, every method is overwhelmed by a −95% collapse.
  • The ablation is the most interesting result: neither ingredient alone helps much in the crisis, and "adaptive only" collapses back to damped Holt (the optimiser sets b ≈ 0 because, without clipping, a large α would chase pre-COVID holiday outliers). Only with clipping can the optimiser afford a positive b. The two ingredients are complementary — that is the core design argument for AR-Holt.
  • In normal operations (Exp A) the adaptive machinery is mostly idle and AR-Holt performs like damped Holt. Holt–Winters (a fully seasonal model whose seasonal pattern keeps updating) is the strongest model in the normal year, and is significantly better than AR-Holt by DM. This is an honest negative result: our fixed weekday indices (estimated once on the last 26 training weeks) cannot follow the slow drift of the weekly pattern over a year, while Holt–Winters updates it every day.
  • Classic series: on AirPassengers AR-Holt is close to the best models; on the annual Australian series there is nothing to adapt to and AR-Holt is not competitive — with only 37 training years the conformal calibration also has few errors, so its intervals are too narrow.
  • Intervals are close to nominal coverage for the daily series in normal times — the conformal calibration works. During COVID every model's 80% intervals under-cover (no method could calibrate on a shock it had never seen), while the 95% intervals stay closer to nominal because the error scale σ_t widens quickly once large errors arrive.

13. Application demo: checkpoint staffing for ATL, next 7 days¶

AR-Holt is fitted on ATL's full history; its 7-day forecast at the 80th percentile (P80, interpolated from the conformal intervals) is spread over the hours of each day with ATL's hourly profile. Security lanes = ⌈passengers per hour ÷ 150⌉, officers = lanes × 3. The throughput and staffing figures are illustrative assumptions, not TSA standards.

In [29]:

fc = m_atl.forecast(7)

14. Conclusions, limitations and future work¶

Conclusions.

  1. AR-Holt — a damped Holt with a tracking-signal-driven smooth-transition α and regime-switching robust clipping — is implemented from scratch, provably nests damped Holt, and has been validated against statsmodels.
  2. During the COVID-19 collapse it was the most accurate method on the combined hub series and on most individual airports, with significant one-step gains over all fixed-parameter smoothing benchmarks.
  3. In a normal year it behaves like damped Holt; the seasonal Holt–Winters benchmark is more accurate there. AR-Holt's value is insurance against shocks, not a free lunch in calm times.
  4. Adaptivity and robustness are complementary: neither helps alone in the crisis.
  5. Locally-adaptive conformal intervals give near-nominal coverage in normal operations without any normality assumption.

Limitations.

  • No explicit holiday effects — Thanksgiving, Christmas and July 4th are treated as outliers rather than predicted; residuals remain autocorrelated and heavy-tailed.
  • Parameters are not refitted online — they are estimated once on the training span. Rolling re-estimation would let the model learn from a shock while it happens.
  • Fixed seasonal indices — the weekday pattern is estimated once and cannot drift (the main reason Holt–Winters wins in the normal year).
  • A sudden step change costs AR-Holt the first 2–3 days, by design (Section 10.4).
  • TSA throughput counts screened departing passengers, not all travellers (no connecting passengers), and the staffing parameters are assumptions.

Future work.

  • Holiday regressors (or holiday-specific seasonal indices) for the U.S. federal calendar.
  • A hierarchical airport → national model with forecast reconciliation, so ALL7 and the seven airport forecasts add up.
  • Online re-estimation of (a, b, β, φ) on a rolling window, and slowly updating seasonal indices.
  • Learning the regime threshold τ from data, or a probabilistic regime model (Markov switching).
